posts.title: Why one accountable team beats five vendors, every time
posts.excerpt: Splitting product, CRM, mobile and AI across four agencies feels safe. It's the fastest way to build a broken system.
posts.author: jules

body.text: Every ambitious business eventually hits the same wall. Marketing builds a site with an agency. Ops picks a CRM with a consultant. Someone in support stitches Zapier flows together at 2am. A year later nothing talks to anything, and the founders spend more time coordinating vendors than growing the company.
The hidden tax of fragmented delivery

Every hand-off between vendors is a translation loss. Every translation loss shows up later as a bug, a duplicated feature, or a data model that has to be rewritten. That's the real cost of a fragmented stack — not the invoices, but the compounding rework.
You don't buy software. You buy the ability to change it later.
What one team actually changes

text: Decisions get made in hours, not weeks of async threads.
One roadmap covers marketing, product, CRM and automation.
Design tokens, auth, and data models are shared across every surface.

body.text: That's the Readyio bet: fewer vendors, more velocity, a system that keeps compounding value instead of debt.

posts.title: Measuring what actually matters: KPIs founders keep getting wrong
posts.excerpt: Dashboards are cheap. Deciding what to put on them is the whole job. A framework we use with every client in the first two weeks.
posts.author: alex

body.text: Most dashboards founders show us have twelve numbers on them and one is quietly wrong. Here's the shortlist we run every engagement.
Start with the one number that describes the business
Everything else is a diagnostic. If the top-line number moves, you should be able to trace it back to two or three inputs — no more.
Retention beats acquisition (almost) every time
A leaky bucket doesn't fill faster with a bigger tap. Fix retention curves before you scale spend.

posts.title: AI agents that actually ship: a pattern that works in production
posts.excerpt: The demo works. The production version breaks on day two. Here's the architecture we use for AI agents that survive real customers.
posts.author: priya

body.text: Anyone can build an AI demo in an afternoon. The hard part is what happens on day two, when real people ask real questions the demo never planned for.
Treat the agent like a product, not a script
It needs a scope, guardrails, telemetry, and an escape hatch to a human. Skip any of those and you don't have a feature, you have a support incident.
The four layers we always ship

text: Retrieval — grounded on your actual docs, not vibes.
Tools — a small, typed set of actions the agent can take.
Guardrails — refusal policies and PII scrubbing at the edge.
Observability — traces, evals, and a feedback loop from real users.

posts.title: Designing mobile experiences that feel native without a native team
posts.excerpt: Cross-platform is a business decision, not a design compromise. Here's how we get 90% of the native feel from a single codebase.
posts.author: alex

body.text: Native-feeling apps aren't about the framework. They're about respecting platform conventions where they matter and ignoring them where they don't.
The 20% of native that matters most
Gestures, haptics, keyboard behavior, and safe areas. Get those right and most users can't tell.

posts.title: The CRM you actually need is smaller than you think
posts.excerpt: Off-the-shelf CRMs punish you for being different. Custom ones can too — if you build the wrong thing. Here's the middle path.
posts.author: jules

body.text: Most CRM projects fail for the same reason: someone tried to model every edge case up front instead of shipping the 20% that runs the business.
Start with the pipeline, not the entities
Model the flow first. The data structures will fall out of it naturally.

posts.title: Shipping culture vs. planning culture: pick one
posts.excerpt: Teams that ship weekly and teams that plan quarterly are playing different games. The choice determines almost everything else.
posts.author: priya

body.text: The teams we admire have a strong bias to action. The teams we get called in to rescue have a strong bias to plans.
Bias to action doesn't mean careless
It means smaller batches, shorter feedback loops, and enough guardrails that a Tuesday mistake isn't a Friday emergency.
